<reason>CON set a usable decision rule (nutrition delivered per available dollar to the children who need it) and then dismantled PRO's three pillars one at a time with mechanisms rather than assertion: direct certification and whole-school/blanket eligibility for take-up, cashless universal serving lines for register stigma, and phase-out bands or a higher threshold for the cliff-edge family. The reframe that PRO's pillars are objections to *bad* means testing rather than to targeting was the debate's most clarifying move, and CON extended it well ("an argument for drawing the line in a better place"). CON also caught a genuine internal tension: PRO's cost defence relied on aggregate eligibility formulas, which require the same income identification PRO wanted to abolish, shrinking the promised administrative windfall. PRO's distinction between back-office funding math and daily public sorting was a fair and fairly good answer, and its durability argument was a real live route, but PRO supported it only with an unspecified appeal to "budget history" and never met CON's sharpest counter-mechanism — that middle-class families genuinely need Social Security but can pack a sandwich, so universal allegiance is shallow, and austerity degrades universal food programs regressively. Most damaging, CON's pressure question demanding a ring-fence commitment on summer feeding, breakfast and food quality produced the concession that budgets aren't infinite and that protection is "how a legislature prioritizes"; CON converted that honestly-given answer into the closing frame of "arithmetic versus hope." PRO's closing crystallized the cliff-relocation and squeezed-vs-cut asymmetry cleanly, but CON had already answered both (a slope is not a cliff; nobody proposed abolishing school lunch, so "zero tray" is a phantom). CON's overlong first rebuttal being clipped is a real execution cost, but the clipped material was substantially re-made later. Both sides kept format discipline with proper Q/A labels; PRO's late claim that CON "never answered my Q2" was chronologically off.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's pressure question demanding PRO promise that "not one dollar" comes out of summer feeding, breakfast, or food quality in high-poverty schools. PRO's honest answer — budgets aren't infinite, it depends on legislative priorities — let CON crystallize the clash as "my objection is arithmetic, PRO answered it with a hope," paired with the regressive-degradation mechanism that a thinner tray costs the child with no fridge everything and the comfortable family nothing.</best_rebuttal>
